catalog_quote: [p.9, sec. 1.3 Tone] Kumam is a tone language, exhibiting a low tone, a high tone, a falling tone, a rising tone, a downstep high tone and a double downstep high tone, which contrast on a phonetic level. However, a low toneme and a high toneme are posited in underlying representations. There are a few tone sandhi rules which have the effect of altering the underlying tonal representation of a word in particular environments. [p.6, sec. 1.2.2] The vowel sandhi rules are applied to unstressed vowels only. When a word ending in a vowel is followed by a word beginning with a vowel, if the vowels are stressed, vowel coalescence does not take place between them. For instance, when the preposition ɪ 'at, in, to' is followed by the noun ɔt 'house', the vowel of the preposition is not deleted because both the vowel of the preposition ɪ 'at, in, to' and that of the noun ɔt 'house' are stressed. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kumam is analysed as a tone language (underlying L and H tonemes; surface L, H, falling, rising, downstep H, double-downstep H). The grammar has no section on stress and never states where word stress falls; 'stress' is invoked only as a blocking condition on vowel sandhi: monosyllabic content words and the preposition ɪ are 'stressed', while grammatical particles (possessive a, attributive a) and the final vowel of disyllabic jamé 'things' are 'not stressed' (which would be consistent with non-final/stem stress, but the author does not say so).
new_statements.exceptions: None; only that pronominal object suffixes and topic boundaries block vowel sandhi independently of stress (p.6-7).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is lexical and grammatical (aspect marked by suprasegmental L morpheme); tone sandhi operates across 'phonological units' (≈ words). The stress remarks concern word-level stress of vowels at word edges in connected speech; p.379 adds that Kumam, as a tone language, does 'not make use of stress to express information structure in most cases'.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Hieda works describe the same variety: Kumam as spoken in Kaberamaido/Soroti/Serere districts, central Uganda (one principal consultant, fieldwork 1999-2012); no dialect differentiation is made. Glottocode kuma1275, ISO kdi.
